claim_verdicts.evidence: git show stage-1:samples/DonHang.Samples/Samples/Design/OrderNotifications.cs: line 11 `private readonly EmailNotifier notifier = new();` in OrderPlacedTightlyCoupled; line 20 `public sealed class OrderNotifications(INotifier notifier)`; lines 20-23 contain no `new`.

refs csharp-12.md: "You can now create primary constructors in any `class` and `struct`. ... Primary constructor parameters are in scope for the entire body of the class." Tutorial: "You can add parameters to a `struct` or `class` declaration to create a *primary constructor*." Projects target net10.0 (C# 14 per versions.yaml), so the feature applies.

OrdersController.cs:12 `public sealed class OrdersController(OrderService orderService, IOrderRepository repository) : ControllerBase`; OrderService.cs:6 `public sealed class OrderService(...)`; IOrderRepository.cs: `public interface IOrderRepository`.

OrderService.cs:6 `public sealed class OrderService(IOrderRepository repository, INotifier notifier)`. The only `new` in the file: `new ArgumentException`, `new Order { ... }`, `new KeyNotFoundException` — none create a repository or notifier. OrdersController's `new` calls are OrderItem/anonymous route values only.

`git grep -n OrderNotifications stage-1` outside the declaring file returns only a comment in DonHang.Domain/INotifier.cs:4. No `new OrderNotifications`/`OrderNotifications(` call anywhere in the repo, samples tests included.

EfOrderRepository.cs:7 `public sealed class EfOrderRepository(DonHangDbContext db) : IOrderRepository`; DonHangDbContext.cs:7 `public sealed class DonHangDbContext(DbContextOptions<DonHangDbContext> options) : DbContext(options)` — concrete (and sealed).

ASP.NET Core DI: "the dependency injection (DI) software design pattern, which is a technique for achieving Inversion of Control (IoC) between classes and their dependencies." Architectural principles: "The practice of *dependency injection* is made possible by following the dependency inversion principle." Injection of a concrete type is shown by OrdersController.cs:12 (OrderService).

Follows directly from the code shape: a field initialiser `= new EmailNotifier()` inside the class fixes the concrete type regardless of the declared field type; changing it requires editing that initialiser. Same point made and reviewed in design.l1.solid-dip.

dotnet architecture/maui DI: "a class constructor is invoked ... any values that the object needs are passed as arguments to the constructor. This is an example of dependency injection known as *constructor injection*." "There are also other types of dependency injection, such as *property setter injection* and *method call injection*, but they are less commonly seen." ASP.NET Core: "## Action injection with `FromServices`" — "enables injecting a service directly into an action method without using constructor injection".

issues.text: Round-1 major (constructor-only DI) is resolved in section 3 and summary line 1, but section 4 and summary line 2 still give 'through the constructor' as THE answer to how DI delivers the object, unqualified. Covered by section 3's 'in this course' framing, so only minor; the round-1 issue text named this sentence too.
issues.quote: DI asks how the object reaches the class, and answers: through the constructor, from outside.
issues.fix: Section 4: "DI asks how the object reaches the class, and answers: from outside, here through the constructor." Summary line 2: "...DI says how the object gets there (from outside, here through the constructor)."

issues.text: The misconception is about constructor parameters that are plain strings or numbers, but the correction uses `orderId` passed to `Handle`, which is a method parameter. I am left not knowing whether a constructor parameter of type `string` or `int` counts as DI, and the Core concepts definition ('receives ... as constructor parameters') seems to say it does.
issues.quote: The `orderId` passed to `Handle` is data the method works on; the `INotifier` is a collaborator it calls `Send` on.
issues.fix: Replace the `orderId` example with a constructor-parameter example, e.g. one sentence saying a constructor parameter of type `int` or `string` is a value the class keeps, not an object whose behaviour it calls, so passing it in is not dependency injection.

issues.text: 'collaborator' is used as if it were a term, contrasted with 'data'. It is not in my vocabulary or Core concepts; I can only guess it means the same as 'dependency'. It appears again in quiz q5 option d's explanation ('not a collaborator').
issues.quote: the `INotifier` is a collaborator it calls `Send` on.
issues.fix: Replace 'collaborator' with 'dependency' (defined in Core concepts) in section 6 and in the q5 explanation for option d.

issues.text: I had to re-read this sentence twice. It does not say why a class creating `EmailNotifier` is tied to it when the field is `INotifier` (the `new` line names the concrete class, so switching means editing it), nor 'has to come from outside' for what purpose. 'usually' also makes me wonder what the unusual way is. Quiz q4 depends on exactly this reasoning.
issues.quote: A class that creates its own `EmailNotifier` is tied to it even when the field's type is `INotifier`, so the concrete object has to come from outside, and injection is how it usually gets there.
issues.fix: Split into two sentences: first say the `new EmailNotifier()` line inside the class still names the concrete class, so changing the channel means editing that class; then say that for the caller to choose instead, the object must be passed in from outside, which is what injection does.

issues.text: Option c and the explanations for c and d name `SmsNotifier` and `NotifierBase`, which this lesson never introduces (and the DIP summary does not mention). I can still pick a, but the explanation for c ('implements INotifier through NotifierBase') confuses me further.
issues.quote: This would matter only when `SmsNotifier` lacked `Send`, but it implements `INotifier` through `NotifierBase`.
issues.fix: Drop the `NotifierBase` mention from the c explanation, e.g. 'An SMS notifier only needs to implement `INotifier`; whether it does is not what stops the switch — the `new EmailNotifier()` line is.'

issues.text: The correct option is almost word for word summary line 1 / the Core concepts definition, so it can be matched by wording without understanding.
issues.quote: It receives its dependencies as constructor parameters instead of creating them
issues.fix: Reword option a, e.g. 'Whoever creates it passes in the objects it uses, so it never writes `new` for them'.

issues.text: The correct option restates summary line 2 almost verbatim ('DIP says what to depend on ... DI says how the object gets there'), so it is recognisable by wording.
issues.quote: False, because inversion says what to depend on and injection says how the object arrives.
issues.fix: Reword option c around the example instead, e.g. 'False: `OrdersController` is injected with `OrderService`, yet does not depend on an abstraction for it.'

issues.text: The explanation for option d calls the "order placed" string 'the subject text'. Nothing in the lesson says it is a subject; I wonder if it is an email subject and whether that matters.
issues.quote: The subject text is data passed to `Send`, not a collaborator.
issues.fix: Replace 'The subject text' with 'The message text'.

skipped_steps: Section 6: misconception about constructor parameters corrected with a method-parameter example (`orderId` passed to `Handle`).
Section 4: 'so the concrete object has to come from outside' — why the class is tied and what 'from outside' achieves are left for the reader to assemble.
